c.tagline: France's Rome — home to the world's best-preserved Roman arena and the birthplace of denim.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard; airport and evening trips carry surcharges. Uber and Bolt also operate in the city.

emergency.note: 112 is the pan-European emergency number reaching police, fire and ambulance; it works from any phone.

hood_landmark.Gambetta: Les Halles de Nîmes covered market

avoid.reason: The western housing estates of Pissevin and Valdegour see drug-related violence and hold no visitor interest.
Pickpocketing spikes around the Arena and station during the ferias; usual awareness at night.

hood_desc: The compact medieval-and-Roman heart of Nîmes, wrapped around the Arena and the Maison Carrée; a warren of pedestrian lanes, squares, boutiques and the covered market — where first-timers should stay to reach every sight on foot.

A lively, multicultural quarter just north of the Old Town around Boulevard Gambetta and Les Halles market; more local and workaday than the tourist core, with good-value eateries and easy access to the centre.

The elegant northwest edge of the centre beside the 18th-century Jardins de la Fontaine, the Temple of Diana and the Tour Magne; leafy, calm and handsome, well suited to travelers who want greenery and quiet a short walk from the monuments.
The area along grand Avenue Feuchères linking the Arena to the train station; a convenient base for TGV and TER arrivals, with practical hotels and a five-minute walk to the Roman core.

A mostly residential quarter just east of the old town, around Rue de Beaucaire and the streets beyond the boulevards; quieter and more local, a practical choice for a longer, calmer stay a ten-minute walk from the Arena.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 8:30 PM, with the T1 TramBus more frequent; evening service is limited, so plan late trips by taxi or ride app.
transit.note: Nîmes has no metro or tram; the Tango network of city buses plus the high-frequency T1 TramBus (a bus-rapid-transit line) covers the city and Nîmes Métropole.
transit.pay: Buy single tickets from the driver or ticket machines, or load a rechargeable Tango card; validate on board. A single ride is about €1.60.

train: Gare de Nîmes (TER + TGV inOui to Paris, Montpellier, Marseille, Lyon)

transit.m: Airport shuttle bus to Nîmes centre, coordinated with Ryanair flights (~30 min)

tip.r: Service is included by law; locals simply round up or leave a few euros (5-10%) for good service.

landmarks: Arènes de Nîmes (Roman Amphitheatre)
Among the best-preserved Roman amphitheaters anywhere, this first-century arena still stages concerts and ferias before twenty thousand spectators.
Maison Carrée
A perfectly intact Roman temple from around 2 AD, its crisp Corinthian columns now UNESCO-listed and glowing honey-gold at sunset.
Jardins de la Fontaine
One of Europe's first public gardens, laid out in 1745 over a sacred spring, with balustraded pools, statuary and shaded terraces.
Tour Magne
The ruined octagonal Roman tower atop Mont Cavalier crowns the Jardins de la Fontaine with panoramic views across the city's rooftops.
Musée de la Romanité
Elizabeth de Portzamparc's shimmering glass-draped museum faces the arena, displaying five thousand Roman artifacts with dazzling contemporary scenography and a rooftop terrace.
Temple de Diane
A romantically ruined Roman sanctuary of mysterious purpose tucked in the Jardins de la Fontaine, beloved by artists since the eighteenth century.
Porte d'Auguste
The Roman gate where the Via Domitia entered the city, its twin arches from 15 BC guarded by a bronze Augustus.
Cathédrale Notre-Dame-et-Saint-Castor
Nîmes's cathedral blends Romanesque frieze carvings of Genesis with later Gothic rebuilding at the heart of the old town's tangled lanes.
Castellum Aquae (Castellum Divisorium)
The rare Roman water tower where the Pont du Gard aqueduct ended, its distribution basin still visible carved into the rock.
Les Halles de Nîmes
A covered market in the old town packed with stalls of Provençal cheese, charcuterie, olives, and produce, busy with locals every morning.

train.note: Gare de Nimes is a short walk south of the Roman arena, while the newer Nimes Pont-du-Gard station sits about 10 km out on the bypass line and is linked by shuttle bus. Around four direct trains a day run to Barcelona in about 3h25m - some are Renfe AVE services booked on renfe.com, others SNCF TGVs on the Paris-Barcelona run booked on SNCF Connect, and the two fare systems are separate. Domestically there are frequent TGV inOui trains to Paris in about 3 hours, Montpellier in 30 minutes, and Marseille, Avignon and Lyon, plus liO regional trains across Occitanie. Check which of the two stations your ticket names before setting out.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the bus station immediately next to Gare de Nimes, so train and coach connections are a two-minute walk. Barcelona takes 6-7 hours by coach against 3h25m by train, so the bus is a price play rather than a time saver. Cars liO regional coaches (https://www.lio-occitanie.fr/) serve Uzes, the Pont du Gard, Ales and the Camargue at a low flat fare paid on board. International tickets are online-only; carry ID for Spanish departures.

ferry.note: Nimes lies about 40 km inland from the Mediterranean and has no port or ferry service. The nearest sailings leave from Sete, roughly an hour away by train, where Corsica Linea runs to Algeria (https://www.corsicalinea.com/) and Corsica Ferries to Corsica, Sardinia and the Balearics (https://www.corsica-ferries.fr/). Marseille, about an hour by TGV, offers a wider choice including Tunisia and Morocco.

half.name: Pont du Gard
half.blurb: The colossal, remarkably intact three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge over the Gardon, ~25 km northeast — Nîmes's must-see excursion.

half.name: Uzès
half.blurb: A honey-stone Renaissance town with an arcaded square (Place aux Herbes) and the Duché castle, ~25 km away.

half.name: Arles
half.blurb: Van Gogh's town, with its own Roman arena and theatre and a famous Saturday market, ~30 km south.

full.name: Camargue & Aigues-Mortes
full.blurb: Wetland wildlife, pink flamingos, white horses and the walled salt town of Aigues-Mortes south toward the sea.
